<reason>Both sides debated at a high level and stayed on the motion's operative comparison. A's route was the word "achievable," backed by a genuinely vivid asymmetry ("PRO's plan requires eighty Gazas; mine requires zero") and a fair attack on B's mechanism as hypothetical (a package no coalition has been offered, a map rejected three times). But A's case had a structural vulnerability that B exploited relentlessly: A's proposed rival — two national communities with separate sovereign institutions on shared land — presupposes two sovereignties, and A's own answer to the Ariel enforcement question ("Palestinian police, under Palestinian law") conceded sovereign Palestinian jurisdiction over Israeli citizens on land Israel no longer governs. B's framing that this is "two states with residency rules attached" is the more natural reading of the motion as written, since confederal models are ordinarily described as two-state variants; A's reply that partition definitionally requires a hard border and mass evacuation was a plausible stipulation but never established over B's reading. B also neutralized A's two best independent lines: the "alibi/mirage" argument was turned on its own prediction (the horizon has faded and occupation deepened rather than lifted), and the polling attack was absorbed by the correct "least bad" reframe (every option polls poorly; binational polls below partition). Decisively, A demanded an actor and mechanism from B but never supplied one for its own plan — B's point that confederation has never been tabled, never polled competitively, and has no constituency in either society was left standing, while A's "recognition is a lighter vote than evacuation" was damaged by B's showing that recognition here means handing criminal jurisdiction over hundreds of thousands of citizens without IDF backing. A made the debate lively and pressed real burdens; B made it easier to decide.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Q2 on who arrests the settler in Ariel, followed by A's answer ("Palestinian police, under Palestinian law") and B's closing use of it: the question forced A either into occupation-with-new-vocabulary or into conceding sovereign Palestinian jurisdiction, which B credibly recast as the motion itself. A's counterpunch — that PRO thereby abandons the border and evacuation that define partition — was the best available reply but did not fully break the collapse.</best_rebuttal>
